blocks.text: Interview problems never say "use a stack". You have to recognise the shape of the problem. The good news is that stack problems give themselves away with a handful of signals.

items: **Matching or nesting.** Brackets, HTML tags, `[` and `]` in an encoded string — anything where the **latest** opening must close first. (Valid Parentheses, Decode String)

**The newest item reacts with the latest survivor.** Each new item may cancel, merge with or destroy the item just before it — and then the one before that. (Asteroid Collision, removing adjacent duplicates)
**Undo, go back, backtrack.** You need to return to the most recent state or choice. (undo, browser history, depth-first search)
**Reverse order.** Something must come out in the opposite order it went in. (reversing, postfix → prefix)

**"The nearest bigger or smaller one".** For each element, find the closest element to its left or right that is larger or smaller. This is the **monotonic stack**, a lesson of its own. (Next Greater Element, Largest Rectangle, Trapping Rain Water)
**Operators waiting for operands.** Evaluating or converting expressions. (prefix, infix and postfix)

blocks.alt: A decision list. Does the most recent item need handling first? Use a stack. Must items be handled in arrival order? Use a queue. Do you need to jump to any position? Use an array. Do you look things up by key? Use a hash map. Do you always need the smallest or largest of everything? Use a heap.
blocks.caption: Ask the first question first — it is the stack signal.

blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string, repeatedly delete two **adjacent equal letters** until no such pair is left. For `"abbaca"`: removing `bb` gives `"aaca"`, then removing `aa` gives `"ca"`.

Which signal is this? When a new letter arrives, it can only cancel the letter **right before it among the survivors** — and after a pair vanishes, the letter before that becomes the neighbour. "The newest item reacts with the latest survivor": a stack.

blocks.alt: Processing abbaca with a stack. a is pushed. b is pushed. The second b matches the top b, so both vanish. The next a matches the top a, so both vanish. c is pushed, then a is pushed. The stack ends as c, a, so the answer is ca.

elements.text: then a meets a: both vanish
elements.originalText: then a meets a: both vanish

blocks.caption: Each letter either cancels the top of the stack or joins it.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** The brute force — scan for a pair, delete it, start over — is O(n²). The stack never re-scans: each letter is pushed once and popped at most once.
When a stack is the wrong tool

items: **You need the oldest item first** — that is a **queue**.
**You need the middle, or the k-th item** — a stack can only see its top. Use an **array**.
**You search for a value** — a stack would have to pop everything to look. Use a **hash set** or **hash map**.
**You need the minimum of everything, often** — a plain stack can't do that in O(1)… unless you add a helper stack, which is exactly the **Design Min & Max Stack** problem.

blocks.alt: The cost of each stack operation. push, pop, peek, isEmpty and size are O(1). Searching for a value is O(n). Reaching the k-th item from the top is O(k), because everything above it must be popped first.

pop()            O(1)
peek()           O(1)

search for x     O(n)   pop until found

items: Reach for a stack when the **most recent unfinished item** must be handled first.
A stack turns "re-scan after every change" (O(n²)) into one pass (O(n)), because each item is pushed and popped at most once.
If you need the oldest item, random access or search, a stack is the wrong tool.
